title: Higher Fees Planned for Taiwan's Highest Mountain Lodges
summaryZh: 國家公園署擬訂新奇萊山屋收費，排雲山莊住宿費調漲。
summaryHi: ताइवान में नए चीलाई पर्वत केबिन पर शुल्क और पाइयुन लॉज का किराया बढ़ाने का प्रस्ताव।
summaryEs: Taiwán propone cobrar en el nuevo refugio de Qilai y subir la tarifa del albergue Paiyun.
summaryJa: 新奇莱山小屋の料金案と、排雲山荘の宿泊料値上げ案が公表された。
summaryKo: 대만이 새 치라이 산장 요금과 파이윈 산장 숙박료 인상안을 발표했다.
summaryEn: Taiwan plans to charge for the new Qilai Mountain Cabin and raise prices at Paiyun Lodge.
paragraphs: Hikers heading for Taiwan's highest peaks may soon have to pay considerably more for a bed, after the National Park Service unveiled proposed fees for two high-altitude lodges on Friday.

At Paiyun Lodge in Yushan National Park, which at 3,402 metres is Taiwan's highest mountain lodge, the nightly rate would more than double from NT$480 per person, a price unchanged since 2013, to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.

The agency also set out charges for the new Qilai Mountain Cabin in Taroko National Park. Located at 3,345 metres in Hualien County, near the Nantou border, the 40-bed cabin has been open on a trial basis since August 21 and is currently free. Guests would pay NT$800 a night on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays.

Officials pointed to the high cost of maintenance and the difficulty of resupplying buildings at such altitudes. The fees would also fund staffing and upgrades such as solar power with energy storage, drying and changing rooms, and charging equipment.
The proposal is open for public consultation for 60 days, and no implementation date has been announced.
Many people in Taiwan like to climb high mountains. They often sleep in small houses on the mountains. These houses are called lodges or cabins.
Now the government wants climbers to pay more money. Paiyun Lodge is on the way to Yushan. Now one night costs NT$480. The new price will be NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.
There is also a new cabin on Qilai Mountain. It has 40 beds. It opened in August, and now it is free. The new price will be NT$800 on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays.
The government says it costs a lot of money to look after these buildings. It is hard to carry food and things up the mountain.
People can give their opinions for 60 days. There is no start date yet.
Taiwan's National Park Service has suggested new prices for two popular mountain lodges, including the country's highest one, Paiyun Lodge in Yushan National Park.
Paiyun Lodge sits at 3,402 metres. A night there has cost NT$480 per person since 2013. Under the new plan, the price would rise to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.

The plan also sets prices for the new Qilai Mountain Cabin in Taroko National Park. The cabin is at 3,345 metres in Hualien County and has 40 beds. It opened for a trial on August 21, and staying there is free at the moment. The proposed price is NT$800 per night on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays.

The agency said looking after buildings so high up is expensive, and bringing supplies is difficult. The money would also pay for staff and new equipment, such as solar power, drying rooms and phone charging.
The public now has 60 days to comment on the plan. No start date has been set.
Hikers heading for Taiwan's highest peaks may soon have to pay considerably more for a bed, after the National Park Service unveiled proposed fees for two high-altitude lodges on Friday.

At Paiyun Lodge in Yushan National Park, which at 3,402 metres is Taiwan's highest mountain lodge, the nightly rate would more than double from NT$480 per person, a price unchanged since 2013, to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.

The agency also set out charges for the new Qilai Mountain Cabin in Taroko National Park. Located at 3,345 metres in Hualien County, near the Nantou border, the 40-bed cabin has been open on a trial basis since August 21 and is currently free. Guests would pay NT$800 a night on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays.

Officials pointed to the high cost of maintenance and the difficulty of resupplying buildings at such altitudes. The fees would also fund staffing and upgrades such as solar power with energy storage, drying and changing rooms, and charging equipment.
The proposal is open for public consultation for 60 days, and no implementation date has been announced.

Climbers bound for Taiwan's loftiest summits could soon face markedly higher overnight costs, after the National Park Service published draft fees for two of the country's most sought-after high-altitude shelters.

The steepest change concerns Paiyun Lodge in Yushan National Park. Perched at 3,402 metres, it is Taiwan's highest mountain lodge, and its rate of NT$480 per person per night has stood untouched since 2013. Under the proposal, it would climb to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.

Meanwhile, the newly built Qilai Mountain Cabin in Taroko National Park, which sits at 3,345 metres in Hualien County and has operated free of charge on a trial basis since August 21, would charge NT$800 on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays. The 40-bed cabin, featuring renewable energy and lightweight construction, replaces an eight-bed predecessor whose bookings were suspended in October 2025.

The agency attributed the increases to the considerable expense of maintenance and the logistical difficulty of resupply at altitude, as well as staffing costs and upgrades including solar power, drying rooms and charging facilities.
The fees are subject to a 60-day public consultation, and no implementation date has yet been set.
Mountaineers in Taiwan may soon encounter substantially higher accommodation costs, following the National Park Service's publication of proposed fees for two prominent high-altitude lodges.

The most significant adjustment would apply to Paiyun Lodge in Yushan National Park. Situated at 3,402 metres, it is the highest mountain lodge in Taiwan, and its nightly charge of NT$480 per person has remained unchanged since 2013. The proposal would raise this to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays, an increase of more than one hundred per cent.

Simultaneously, fees would be introduced at the new Qilai Mountain Cabin in Taroko National Park. Located at 3,345 metres in Hualien County, the 40-bed facility has been operating free of charge on a trial basis since August 21. Under the plan, guests would pay NT$800 on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays. Notably, the cabin relies on renewable energy and lightweight construction in order to minimise its environmental footprint.

The agency justified the changes by citing the substantial cost of maintenance and the logistical challenges of resupply at altitude, together with expenditure on staffing and infrastructure upgrades, such as solar power, drying rooms and charging equipment.
The proposed fees will undergo a 60-day public consultation, and an implementation date has yet to be confirmed.
